## Introduction

This page covers some additional Slurm topics that build on the
[w10a](../week10/w10a_slurm1.qmd) and [w10b](../week10/w10b_slurm2.qmd) lectures:
more `sbatch` options, Slurm environment variables, copying Slurm log files to output dirs,
interactive shell jobs, customizing `squeue` output, checking how many resources your jobs used,
and ways to automate multi-step workflows with Bash and Slurm.

To run the commands on this page yourself, start a VS Code session at
<https://ondemand.osc.edu> in `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER`, as per usual.

## More `sbatch` options

### Requesting large amounts of memory

The maximum amount of memory you can request on **regular** Pitzer compute nodes
is 178 GB.
If you need more than that, there are **specialized** `largemem` or `hugemem` nodes.

Switching to such a node generally happens automatically based on your requested
amount.
Unfortunately,
there are "**gaps**" between the maximum and minimum amounts of RAM on these node types,
which means that certain amounts of memory cannot be requested on any node
(see [this OSC page](https://www.osc.edu/resources/technical_support/supercomputers/pitzer/batch_limit_rules)
for details on Pitzer nodes).

To make sure that a batch job runs on one of these node types,
you can also request it explicitly with the `--partition` option. For example:

```{.bash .file filename="myscript.sh (excerpt)"}
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --partition=hugemem
#SBATCH --mem=900G
```

### Separating standard output and standard error

By default, both _stdout_ and _stderr_ end up in the same Slurm log file,
but you can **separate them** into different files with the `--error` option, e.g.:

```{.bash .file filename="myscript.sh (excerpt)"}
#SBATCH --output=slurm-fastqc-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=slurm-fastqc-%j.err
```

In the above example, only _stdout_ will go into the file specified with `--output`,
and _stderr_ will go into the file specified with `--error`.
Separating _stdout_ and _stderr_ like that could be useful because it may make
it easier to spot errors,
and an empty `--error` file would mean that there were no errors.

However, reality is more messy:
some programs print their main output (results) not to a file but to standard out,
in which case all logging output, i.e. errors and regular messages alike,
is designated as standard error.
And some other programs use _stdout_ for all messages.
Therefore, with Slurm, I **personally** only specify `--output`,
such that both _stdout_ and _stderr_ end up in that file.

### Get warned when your job is close to its time limit

You may also find the `--mail-type` values `TIME_LIMIT_90`, `TIME_LIMIT_80`,
and `TIME_LIMIT_50` useful for very long-running jobs,
which will warn you when the job is at 90/80/50% of the time limit.
This can be useful because you can email OSC to ask for an extension on individual jobs.
You shouldn't do this often, but if you have a job that ran for 6 days and it
looks like it may time out, this may well be worth it.

```{.bash .file filename="myscript.sh (excerpt)"}
#SBATCH --mail-type=TIME_LIMIT_90,FAIL
```

## Slurm environment variables

Slurm automatically makes a number of environment variables available
inside a shell script that you submit as a batch job, such as:

| Variable               | Corresponding option | Description                                                       |
| ---------------------- | -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `$SLURM_JOB_ID`        | ---                   | Job ID assigned by Slurm                                          |
| `$SLURM_JOB_NAME`      | `--job-name`         | Job name (by default, the name of the script)                     |
| `$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK` | `--cpus-per-task`    | Number of reserved cores<br>(only set if you used `--cpus-per-task`) |
| `$SLURM_MEM_PER_NODE`  | `--mem`              | Amount of reserved memory in MB<br>(only set if you used `--mem`)    |
| `$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR`    | ---                   | Path to the dir from which the job was submitted                  |
| `$TMPDIR`              | ---                   | Path to fast temporary storage on the compute node<br>(set by OSC, not Slurm) |

: {.striped .hover tbl-colwidths="[24,22,54]"}

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

As an example of how these environment variables can be useful,
compare these two ways of telling the program STAR how many threads to use.
First, hardcoding the number of threads,
which means the number has to be specified twice:

```{.bash .file filename="star.sh (excerpt)"}
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8

STAR --runThreadN 8 --genomeDir [...]
```

Second, using `$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK`,
so that the number is only specified once, in the Slurm option:

```{.bash .file filename="star.sh (excerpt)"}
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8

STAR --runThreadN "$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK" --genomeDir [...]
```

With the second strategy, you will automatically use the correct (requested)
number of cores, and don't risk having a mismatch.
Also, if you need to change the number of cores, you'll only have to modify it
in one place.

::: callout-warning
#### These variables don't always exist
As noted in the table, some of these variables are only set if you used the corresponding option:
for example, `$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK` doesn't exist if you didn't use `--cpus-per-task`.
And when you run a script with `bash` instead of `sbatch`, they either don't exist,
or, in a VS Code terminal at OSC, contain the values of your VS Code job
(which is a Slurm job too!).
When a variable doesn't exist, `set -u` will make your script stop with an "unbound variable" error.

To avoid this, provide a default value using
[parameter expansion](shell-scripting.qmd#parameter-expansion-to-provide-default-values):

```{.bash .file filename="star.sh (excerpt)"}
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8

# Use the number of reserved cores, or 1 if $SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK doesn't exist
cores="${SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK:-1}"

STAR --runThreadN "$cores" --genomeDir [...]
```

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

:::

You can also use these variables to record a job's resources in its Slurm log file,
which is useful when you look back at the log file later.
For example, in the initial logging section of your script:

```{.bash .file filename="scripts/fastqc.sh (excerpt)"}
echo "Slurm job ID:       ${SLURM_JOB_ID:-none}"
echo "Number of cores:    ${SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK:-1}"
```

## Copying the Slurm log file to the output dir

In [w10b](../week10/w10b_slurm2.qmd#submit-a-job-for-each-file),
you moved your Slurm log files into a `logs` subdir of the output dir by hand,
after checking them.

You may wonder why you shouldn't simply include a dir in the `--output` path, e.g.
`#SBATCH --output=results/fastqc/logs/slurm-fastqc-%j.out`,
so that log files don't have to be moved manually after the job has finished.
But this has two disadvantages:

- **The dir must already exist when you submit the job.**\
  Slurm creates the log file when the job starts,
  before any line of your script has run, and it won't create missing dirs for you.
  So, a `mkdir -p` line inside the script would come too late:
  the job would fail right away, and **no log file would be created at all** ---
  leaving you with nowhere to look to find out what went wrong.
  You'd instead need a `mkdir -p` line right above your `sbatch` command(s)
  in your protocol Markdown file.

- **It's good to do the manual work.**\
  When log files show up in your working dir,
  you'll notice them, and that is a reminder to check them
  for errors before moving them to their final location.
  When they quietly end up elsewhere,
  it's easier to forget about a job and never check whether it succeeded.

Instead, your script itself can put a **copy** of its Slurm log file in the output dir.
The original log file will then still show up in your working dir,
so you'll notice it and check it ---
but afterwards, you can simply delete it,
since a copy is already stored alongside the outputs.
To do this, add the following lines to the very end of your script:

```{.bash .file filename="scripts/fastqc.sh (excerpt)"}
# Copy the Slurm log file to the output dir (only when running as a batch job)
if [[ "$0" == */slurm_script ]]; then
    log_file=$(scontrol show job "$SLURM_JOB_ID" | grep "StdOut=" | cut -d "=" -f 2)
    mkdir -p "$outdir"/logs
    cp "$log_file" "$outdir"/logs/
fi
```

How this works:

- `[[ "$0" == */slurm_script ]]` checks whether the script runs as a batch job.
  `$0` contains the path of the script that is running,
  and in a batch job, Slurm runs a copy of your script called `slurm_script`
  (which is why error messages in Slurm log files mention a path like
  `/var/spool/slurmd/job37615711/slurm_script`).
  (Checking whether `$SLURM_JOB_ID` exists wouldn't work:
  it is also set in your VS Code terminal, because your VS Code session is a Slurm job.)
  See also [this section on `if` statements](shell-scripting.qmd#conditionals).
- `scontrol show job` prints information about a job,
  including a line `StdOut=<path>` with the path to its Slurm log file.
  `grep` selects that line, and `cut` extracts the part after the `=`.
  Because the path comes from Slurm,
  this works no matter how you named your log files with `--output`.

Two things to note:

- Put these lines at the very end of the script,
  after the final "Successfully finished" logging lines,
  because the copy will only contain what was printed up to that point.
- If the script fails, it stops before it reaches these lines (thanks to `set -e`),
  so no copy is made.
  That's actually useful:
  copies in your output dirs only exist for jobs that succeeded,
  while the log files of failed jobs only end up in your working dir,
  where you'll notice them.

## Interactive shell jobs

Interactive shell jobs will grant you interactive shell access on a compute node.
When you use the VS Code app in OnDemand,
your terminal already runs in an interactive job on a compute node!
And if you need more cores for that job, you can request them in the OnDemand form.

But when you work in a plain shell on a login node instead,
for example when you [connect to OSC with SSH](ssh.qmd) from your own computer,
you need to start an interactive shell job yourself
before you can run anything substantial.
You can do so with Slurm's `srun` command[^1],
to which you add `--pty /bin/bash` to get an interactive Bash shell.

[^1]: Other options: `salloc` works almost identically to `srun`,
      whereas `sinteractive` is an OSC convenience wrapper but with more limited options.

To try this, open a login-node shell in OnDemand via
`Clusters` > `Pitzer Shell Access`.
Then, request an interactive shell job, e.g. with 5 cores for 2 hours:

```bash
srun --account=PAS3493 --cpus-per-task=5 --time=120 --pty /bin/bash
```
```bash-out
srun: job 56706630 queued and waiting for resources
srun: job 56706630 has been allocated resources
[jelmer@p0133 ~]$
```

First, some Slurm scheduling info was printed to screen:
initially, the job was queued, and then it was "allocated resources".
Then, you got a new prompt, which shows the name of the compute node your job runs on
(here, `p0133`, whereas before, the prompt showed a login node, like `pitzer-login01`).
Any commands you now type will run in this job, with its 5 cores.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
Don't run `srun` from a VS Code terminal at OSC.
Your VS Code session is a Slurm job itself,
so `srun` will try to run _inside_ that job instead of starting a new one.
If you ask for more cores than your VS Code job has,
it will keep printing "_step creation temporarily disabled_" (press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd> to stop it).
:::

When you're done, type `exit` to end the job and go back to your original shell.
Otherwise, the job will keep running (and using your project's compute hours)
until it reaches its time limit.

## Monitoring your jobs with `squeue`

### Choosing which columns to show

The default columns of `squeue -u $USER -l` are quite narrow:
for example, job names are cut off after 8 characters.
That is a problem when you have many jobs with long names,
such as the jobs that a Nextflow pipeline submits.
With the `--format` option, you can choose which columns to show, and how wide they are:

```bash
squeue -u $USER --format="%.9i %.9P %.100j %.8T %.10M %.10l %.4C %R %.16V"
```
```bash-out
    JOBID PARTITION                                                                                                 NAME    STATE       TIME TIME_LIMIT CPUS NODELIST(REASON)      SUBMIT_TIME
 42175824       cpu                 nf-NFCORE_RNASEQ_RNASEQ_FASTQ_QC_TRIM_FILTER_SETSTRANDEDNESS_SORTMERNA_(S79)  RUNNING       0:53   16:00:00   17 p0111 2026-11-30T08:49
 42175780       cpu          nf-NFCORE_RNASEQ_PREPARE_GENOME_STAR_GENOMEGENERATE_(GCF_016801865.2_TS_CPP_V2_genomic.fna)  RUNNING       3:19   16:00:00   17 p0116 2026-11-30T08:46
 42175708       cpu                                                                                        nfc-rnaseq.sh  RUNNING       5:19   12:00:00    1 p0222 2026-11-30T08:44
```

Each `%` code in the `--format` string is one column,
and the number before the letter sets the column's width:
for example, `%.100j` shows the job name in a 100-character-wide column.
(The `.` makes the text right-aligned.)
These are the codes used above, plus a few other useful ones:

| Code | Column                                                               |
| ---- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `%i` | Job ID                                                               |
| `%P` | Partition                                                            |
| `%j` | Job name                                                             |
| `%T` | Job state (e.g. `PENDING` or `RUNNING`)                              |
| `%M` | For how long the job has been running                                |
| `%l` | Time limit                                                           |
| `%C` | Number of reserved cores                                             |
| `%R` | When running: the node(s) it runs on;<br>when pending: why it is pending |
| `%V` | When the job was submitted                                           |
| `%m` | Amount of reserved memory                                            |
| `%S` | When the job started, or for pending jobs, when it is expected to start |

: {.striped .hover}

For a full list of codes, see the `--format` section in the manual (`man squeue`).

### Other useful `squeue` options

- To see when your pending jobs are **expected to start**, use `--start`
  (Slurm's estimates are often rough, and may change as other jobs are submitted):

  ```bash
  squeue -u $USER --start
  ```

- To **count** your jobs, for example how many of them are still pending,
  combine `-t` with `-h` (no header line) and `wc -l`:

  ```bash
  squeue -u $USER -t PENDING -h | wc -l
  ```

- To only show **specific jobs**, use `-j` with one or more job IDs, e.g.
  `squeue -j 42175708,42175780`.

To avoid having to type the long `--format` command,
you can [make an alias](#aliases-for-long-job-monitoring-commands) for it.

## Checking your jobs' resource usage

To choose sensible values for `--time`, `--mem`, and `--cpus-per-task`,
it helps to know how much of each your earlier jobs actually used.
For example, after running a program for one or a few samples,
you can use this information to adjust the requests for the remaining samples.

### `seff`: resource usage of a finished job

The easiest way to check a job's resource usage is with `seff`
("Slurm efficiency"), which takes a job ID as its only argument:

```bash
seff 37615718
```
```bash-out
Job ID: 37615718
Cluster: pitzer
User/Group: jelmer/PAS0471
State: COMPLETED (exit code 0)
Cores: 1
CPU Utilized: 00:00:08
CPU Efficiency: 80.00% of 00:00:10 core-walltime
Job Wall-clock time: 00:00:10
Memory Utilized: 245.32 MB
Memory Efficiency: 5.38% of 4.45 GB
```

The most useful lines are:

- **`State`** --- whether the job completed successfully
  (see [the section on `sacct`](#sacct-an-overview-of-many-jobs) for other states).
- **`CPU Efficiency`** --- how much of the reserved cores' time was actually used.
  A low percentage for a job with multiple cores means that the program didn't use all of them.
  For example, a FastQC job for a single file with 4 cores would get no more than 25%:
  recall the [FastQC exercise in w10b](../week10/w10b_slurm2.qmd#modify-the-script-for-usage-with-slurm).
- **`Memory Utilized`** --- the peak memory use,
  which `Memory Efficiency` compares to the amount of memory you had available.
  If a job failed and this is close to 100%, it likely ran out of memory.
- **`Job Wall-clock time`** --- how long the job ran,
  which you can compare to the time limit you set with `--time`.

Only use `seff` after a job has finished:
for running jobs, the numbers are incomplete.

::: {.callout-note}
#### `osc-seff` for GPU jobs
OSC also has its own version of this command,
[`osc-seff`](https://www.osc.edu/resources/getting_started/osc_custom_commands/osc_seff),
which additionally reports GPU usage for jobs that used GPUs.
:::

### `sacct`: an overview of many jobs

When you've submitted many jobs, `sacct` gives you a table with one row per job,
including jobs that have already finished:

```bash
sacct -X
```
```bash-out
JobID           JobName  Partition    Account  AllocCPUS      State ExitCode
------------ ---------- ---------- ---------- ---------- ---------- --------
37615614     ondemand/+        cpu    pas0471          1    RUNNING      0:0
37615705       sleep.sh        cpu    pas0471          1    TIMEOUT      0:0
37615718      fastqc.sh        cpu    pas0471          1  COMPLETED      0:0
37615719      fastqc.sh        cpu    pas0471          1  COMPLETED      0:0
37615720      fastqc.sh        cpu    pas0471          1     FAILED      1:0
# [...output truncated...]
```

- By default, `sacct` shows your own jobs that started since midnight.
  To go back further, use `--starttime`, e.g. `--starttime=2026-10-26`.
- `-X` (`--allocations`) shows one line per job.
  Without it, each job also gets lines for its "job steps", like `.batch` and `.extern`.
- For a single job, use `-j`, e.g. `sacct -X -j 37615720`.

These are the most common values in the `State` column:

| State           | Meaning                                                      |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `COMPLETED`     | The script finished with exit status 0 (no error)            |
| `FAILED`        | The script stopped with an error (see the `ExitCode` column) |
| `TIMEOUT`       | The job was killed because it reached its time limit         |
| `OUT_OF_MEMORY` | The job was killed because it reached its memory limit       |
| `CANCELLED`     | The job was canceled, e.g. with `scancel`                    |

: {.striped .hover}

::: callout-tip
#### Another reason to use `set -e`
A shell script's exit status is that of the last command it ran.
So, without `set -e`, a script in which a command fails halfway
may still end with exit status 0,
and Slurm would list the job as `COMPLETED`.
With `set -euo pipefail`, the script stops at the failing command,
and the job is correctly listed as `FAILED`.
:::

To list only the jobs that did **not succeed**, use `--state`.
In that case, you always have to specify `--starttime` too ---
otherwise, `sacct` only lists jobs that are in one of these states right now:

```bash
sacct -X --starttime=2026-10-26 --state=FAILED,TIMEOUT,OUT_OF_MEMORY,CANCELLED
```
```bash-out
JobID           JobName  Partition    Account  AllocCPUS      State ExitCode
------------ ---------- ---------- ---------- ---------- ---------- --------
37615705       sleep.sh        cpu    pas0471          1    TIMEOUT      0:0
37615720      fastqc.sh        cpu    pas0471          1     FAILED      1:0
```

Finally, you can choose which columns to show with `--format`.
For example, to add a column with each job's run time (`Elapsed`),
and to make the `JobName` column wider so that long job names are not cut off:

```bash
sacct -X --format=JobID,JobName%15,State,ExitCode,Elapsed
```
```bash-out
JobID                JobName      State ExitCode    Elapsed
------------ --------------- ---------- -------- ----------
37615614     ondemand/sys/d+    RUNNING      0:0   00:21:32
37615705            sleep.sh    TIMEOUT      0:0   00:01:11
37615718           fastqc.sh  COMPLETED      0:0   00:00:10
37615719           fastqc.sh  COMPLETED      0:0   00:00:11
37615720           fastqc.sh     FAILED      1:0   00:00:02
# [...output truncated...]
```

- Column names are separated by commas, without spaces.
- `%15` after a column name sets that column's width to 15 characters
  (by default, most columns are 10 characters wide,
  which is why the name of the OnDemand job was cut off to `ondemand/+` above).

### `sstat`: running jobs

`seff` and `sacct` only give complete information after a job has finished.
To check the memory use of a job _while it is running_
(e.g. if you're worried that it may run out of memory), use `sstat`:

```bash
sstat -j 37615800.batch --format=JobID,MaxRSS,AveCPU
```
```bash-out
JobID            MaxRSS     AveCPU
------------ ---------- ----------
37615800.ba+   2405304K   00:02:19
```

Here, `MaxRSS` is the peak memory use so far.
Note the `.batch` after the job ID: `sstat` reports on job "steps",
and the main step of a batch job is called `batch`.

### Aliases for long job monitoring commands

Because you won't remember all of these formatting options,
and even if you do, you don't want to type them out,
this is a case where aliases are really handy. For instance:

```sh
alias sq='squeue -u $USER --format="%.9i %.9P %.100j %.8T %.10M %.10l %.4C %R %.16V"'
alias sact='sacct -X --format=JobID,JobName%15,State,ExitCode,Elapsed'
alias sst='sstat --format=JobID,MaxRSS,AveCPU'
```

You can then add other options when you use an alias, for example:

```sh
sq -t PENDING
```

```sh
sact -j 123456
```

```sh
sst -j 123456.batch
```

An alias only lasts for the current shell session,
so to make them always available in interactive sessions,
add the lines to your Bash configuration file `~/.bashrc`.
See the page on [configuring your shell](shell-config.qmd)
for more on [`~/.bashrc`](shell-config.qmd#shell-configuration-files)
and [aliases](shell-config.qmd#aliases).

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
Aliases are not available in scripts,
so make sure to write out the full commands in scripts
(e.g. your Slurm batch job scripts).
:::

### `/usr/bin/time` and `$SECONDS` in a script

To measure the run time and peak memory use of a single command in a script,
put `/usr/bin/time` in front of it.
Its `-f` option sets what to report, and `-o` writes the report to a file.
For example, `%E` is the run time and `%M` the peak memory use in KB:

```{.bash .file filename="scripts/fastqc.sh (excerpt)"}
# Run FastQC, and store its run time and peak memory use in a file:
/usr/bin/time -f "%E %M" -o "$outdir"/time.txt \
    apptainer exec "$CONTAINER" fastqc --outdir "$outdir" "$fastq"

# Print the run time, and the peak memory use converted from KB to GB:
awk '{printf "Run time: %s    Peak memory: %.2f GB\n", $1, $2 / 1024 / 1024}' "$outdir"/time.txt
```

This will add a line like the following to your Slurm log file:

```bash-out-solo
Run time: 0:09.85    Peak memory: 0.24 GB
```

(The `awk` command reads the two numbers from the file,
and prints them with some text, dividing the memory by 1024 twice to go from KB to GB:
see the [`awk` section](shell-data-tools.qmd#awk-for-tabular-data-processing)
of the self-study page on shell data tools to learn more.
And to get a long list of statistics, use `/usr/bin/time -v` instead.)

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Use the full path `/usr/bin/time` rather than just `time`:
plain `time` runs a simpler, built-in Bash version
that can't report memory use and doesn't have the `-f` and `-o` options.
:::

Finally, to report how long your whole script took to run,
you can use `$SECONDS`:
a special Bash variable that contains the number of seconds since the script started.
For example, add this line to the end of your script:

```{.bash .file filename="scripts/fastqc.sh (excerpt)"}
echo "This script ran for $SECONDS seconds"
```

## Automating multi-step workflows

In [w10b](../week10/w10b_slurm2.qmd#how-about-automation),
you saw that you can't run all the code in a Markdown protocol at once,
because most steps need the output of an earlier step.
This section shows a few ways to automate such a workflow further with Bash and Slurm.
But keep in mind that each of them makes your scripts more complex,
and that a workflow management system like Nextflow is often a better investment of your time.

### Combining steps in one script

At the extreme, you could write a single shell script with a loop for each step,
and submit it as a single batch job.
While this would work, it would be inefficient:
the sample-wise steps would run one sample after the other,
instead of simultaneously in separate batch jobs.

A more reasonable approach is to write
**scripts that process one sample, but run as many steps as possible** for that sample.
However, what if you need to redo only the steps from the middle of your workflow onwards,
e.g. because you want to change some settings there?
Rerunning your all-inclusive script would mean rerunning all steps,
which could be a big waste of time.

#### `if` statements

You could overcome this with `if` statements that only run certain steps,
for example:

```{.bash .file filename="scripts/trim_and_map.sh (excerpt)"}
# Copy the placeholder variables
fastq_r1="$1"
fastq_r2="$2"
run_trim="$3"   # true or false
run_map="$4"    # true or false

# Step 1: Read trimming
if [[ "$run_trim" == true ]]; then
    bash scripts/trim.sh "$fastq_r1" "$fastq_r2" results/trim
fi

# Step 2: Mapping the trimmed reads
if [[ "$run_map" == true ]]; then
    trimmed_r1=results/trim/$(basename "$fastq_r1")
    trimmed_r2=results/trim/$(basename "$fastq_r2")
    bash scripts/map.sh "$trimmed_r1" "$trimmed_r2" results/map
fi
```

Then, to only rerun the mapping step for a sample:

```{.bash .norun}
sbatch scripts/trim_and_map.sh \
  data/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz data/fastq/S63_R2.fastq.gz false true
```

To learn more about `if` statements,
see [this section](shell-scripting.qmd#conditionals)
of the self-study page on shell scripting.

#### Script options

As you can see above, it quickly becomes hard to tell
what each "positional" argument (like `$3` and `$4`) means,
and it's easy to mix them up.
Instead, you can write your script such that it accepts options, e.g.:

```{.bash .norun}
sbatch scripts/trim_and_map.sh \
  --skip_trim data/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz data/fastq/S63_R2.fastq.gz
```

To learn how to do this,
see [this section](shell-scripting.qmd#shell-script-options)
of the self-study page on shell scripting.

### Slurm job dependencies

With the `--dependency` option,
you can submit all jobs at once,
but tell Slurm that a job should only start after the jobs whose outputs it needs
have successfully finished.
For that, you need the job IDs of those earlier jobs.
The `--parsable` option makes `sbatch` print only the job ID
(instead of `Submitted batch job <job-id>`),
which you can store in a variable with
[command substitution](shell-scripting.qmd#command-substitution):

```{.bash .norun}
map_ids=""

for fastq_r1 in data/fastq/*_R1.fastq.gz; do
    fastq_r2=${fastq_r1/_R1/_R2}

    # Submit the trimming job and store its job ID:
    trim_id=$(sbatch --parsable scripts/trim.sh "$fastq_r1" "$fastq_r2" results/trim)

    # Submit the mapping job, which will only start once the trimming job
    # has successfully finished (`afterok`), and store its job ID too:
    trimmed_r1=results/trim/$(basename "$fastq_r1")
    trimmed_r2=results/trim/$(basename "$fastq_r2")
    map_id=$(sbatch --parsable --dependency=afterok:"$trim_id" \
        scripts/map.sh "$trimmed_r1" "$trimmed_r2" results/map)

    # Add the mapping job ID to a colon-separated list of all of them:
    map_ids="$map_ids:$map_id"
done

# The counting job will only start once ALL mapping jobs have successfully finished:
sbatch --dependency=afterok"$map_ids" scripts/count.sh results/map results/count_table.txt
```

If a job fails, the jobs that depend on it will never start.
They may remain in the queue as `PENDING`, with `DependencyNeverSatisfied` as the reason,
until you cancel them with `scancel`.
